J'ai beaucoup aimé ce jeu. J'ai trouvé la première pièce franchement glauque, mais ce n'était plus le cas par la suite. L'histoire est intéressante et l'ambiance est plutôt bien rendue. 
Ce que j'ai principalement apprécié sont les jeux d'objets cachés : moins d'objets à trouver, mais mieux cachés. Le jeu bonus est également particulièrement bon : c'est un vrai jeu de la même qualité que le jeu principal.

Sacra Terra: Angelic Night is not the worst hidden object game I have ever played, but I just don't feel like it's worth your time. Poor translations, a really dated and subpar navigation system, and a puzzling story really make this just kind of average.

The art, the atmosphere, and the puzzles for the most part are all serviceable. There are cutscenes in the game that are well animated. This takes place in a rundown asylum or hospital of some kind, and the setting and environments were interesting at least.

The music is mostly the same track that played throughout the whole game, but oddly it really grew on me. There is a kind of strange charm to it and it ended up being one of the aspects of the game that I like the most.

But between the puzzles and music were frustrations that just compounded for me over time. This is a really personal issue for me, but I play these games mostly on a tablet before bed as a way to unwind and the touch mechanics for the game just really don't work well. I know this is not a fair criticism since many of these games were programmed well before touchscreen interfaces were popular or common, but many other hidden object games I play don't seem to have an issue with this. In this game, touching the screen only seemed to hover the cursor, and in order to select something you had to "double-click" on the part of the screen you wanted to touch, and I found this annoying. I used the trackpad for most of the game instead, but even that had issues, as the game does have some sections where you need to click and drag things to reposition or rotate them in puzzles, and clicking and dragging on a trackpad is awkward and hard to do.

That aside though, the biggest issue I in the game was with the map. You can bring up a map, but there is no dedicated map button in the HUD while exploring, you have to open the notes and then click the map tab in the notebook. I rarely needed to consult the notes, but I frequently had to look at the map and the extra steps to view it become incredibly frustrating as the game wore on. Another issue with the map, while most games allow you to travel to a location by clicking it on the map, this game does not. You cannot just move to a location directly from the map (or if you can, i could never find a way to do it!) so this also meant a lot of lengthy backtracking. The individual locations are all fine, well detailed, finely illustrated, but the ways that locations connect is really hard to intuit. Many games have some kind of a tell on screens that help you understand which direction you're moving, like you may enter a basement and so the next screen may be you looking down the last couple of stairs into the basement. Or you might take a boat across a lake and then next screen has a dock in the background and you know that's the direction you just came from. A lot of this game is disjointed and doesn't do a good job of clarifying which direction you are coming from or going. Part of why I needed the map so much is because the layout of the map is very confusing to me. One part of the game has a generic house hallway, and the doors to either side will move you into yet another generic house hallway. There are all sorts of instances like that in the game where either locations look very similar, or they look so different that it's hard to remember where you just came from.

The hidden object puzzles were mostly fine, I kind of liked them. I didn't find any of them very egregiously hard, and usually they had one multi-step item that required another object to collect and the rest are all normal items in the scene. I had some gripes about these too though, often in games like these, searching the same location of the puzzle multiple times will remove items you already collected previously from the scene. This is a nice touch and makes the game feel more authentic and more professional. I just always thought it was a nice touch, but in this game objects you already collecting just come back the next time you play a hidden object puzzle at that location and I thought it was weird. The other issue was, there are a lot of misnamed items in the puzzles. Frequently as an example, the game would insist that a pistol is a "Musket." I am not a firearm expert by any means, but as an American I am familiar with the term and to me this is a long-barrel gun similar to a rifle (but muskets are smooth-bore barrels, which is why a musket is NOT a rifle, rifles have, you guessed it, riffles barrels.) But the point I am trying to make is, someone trying to find a musket in a hidden object scene is looking for a [i]long[/i] firearm, not a short one like a pistol. There might have been a pistol-sized musket, as I say I am not an expert, but I think it's fair to say most people will be looking for a firearm longer than a pistol when they are looking for a musket. There are other examples that I cannot recall off the top of my head of things just being named incorrectly in the puzzles and this always annoys me since usually the scenes are so specific about which object is the correct one, it's not uncommon for there to be red herrings in the scene to increase the difficulty, so it really is important to be as specific and accurate as possible.

Other than that, a few sections of the game also had the kinds of issues you'd expect; an object you think can be used in a certain situation is wrong and the correct one is unintuitive, or sometimes a part of a scene that looks really innocuous and unimportant will end up being an item you missed but that doesn't really call any attention to itself. These weren't that bad, but although I did not use hints, I was glad that I did play on a difficulty that allowed for me to use the map to see where I had actions available or I think this game would have taken me twice as long.

The story seemed interesting, but at the same time I always felt like I was missing something, like there was a cutscene that I missed maybe, or there was some kind of backstory that I didn't understand. The ending in particular just kind of.. happened and I wasn't sure what if anything it meant for my character. Nothing really seemed to resolve for the person I was playing as. But at the very least it seemed cool from all of the items and documents I found during the game.

The game does have collectibles, but no achievements for collecting them--there are no achievements at all actually, so feel free to use hints or any other tools you want like checking the map since there will be no penalty if you just want to get through the game in a reasonable amount of time. I did find myself wishing that the HUD or map did give you a clue about which locations still had collectibles though because it's easy to miss one and then spend a lot of time backtracking an examining every room to try and find which one you missed. Because I did that, that's exactly what happened to me. And although there are no achievements as I said, I will say that there is something you get for collecting all of the morphing objects but will not spoil what that is, so you may want to if you were planning to skip them for lack of an achievement.

And lastly, there is also a bonus story you can unlock after completing the main game, and it was fun enough, not super long, felt like just the right size.

I guess I would say, if you are just going to use hints to get around and are only playing for puzzles, you could choose a worse game, but the weak aspects of it make me hesitant to recommend it over other games that have better a better story, a better map and navigation, and other quality of life improvements.

I really wanted to enjoy this one, but it just didn’t work for me.

The game feels clunky and dated, and while the story starts with some promise, it never managed to keep me engaged long enough to overcome its shortcomings.

There are far too many hidden-object scenes, to the point of becoming tedious — and I’m someone who does not enjoy HO segments beyond a certain dose.
The puzzles outside of that are extremely easy, predictable, and lacking imagination, offering little sense of challenge or reward.

The map shows where actions are available, but unfortunately doesn't teleport, which means constant backtracking with very little payoff.

In the end, the combination of repetitive HO scenes, overly simple puzzles, and a story that never really captured me led me to quit halfway through.

If you buy it, do so knowing its age, limitations, and dated design.
It may appeal to fans of old-school HO-heavy games, but it wasn’t for me.

A skip for most — unless you're specifically craving vintage-style HOPA.

For a 15 year game this is pretty good. The not so good parts: like many of the HOG games of this era the hidden object games you end up "finding" the same objects in different scenes over and over again, and this is no different. The HO aspect became quite tedious and the graphics are appropriate for the year it was made which is a bit naff. The game also felt quite rushed at the end. The good parts: its an intriguing story and the scenes unfold quite well and in surprising ways which helped the pacing and kept my interest, something that's sorely missing in HOGs these days. for £1.99 its definitely worth the price and I'm going to look at the other games the company made, as the attention to detail and art work was excellent, and I have literally exhausted all of my old Big fish Games library. If you are looking for similar games, try: Shadow Lake (Mystery Case Files), Ravenhearst games, The 13th Skull (my fave game), Phantasmat, Dreadful Tales, Fright (excellent for its age), Maze: Subject 360, Madame Fate, The Dalimar Legacy (play after the Ravenhearst games), Mystery Expedition Prisoners of Ice, Witches Legacy (the first one)

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Ein grundsolides Wimmelbild-Adventure, thematisch angesiedelt bei Engel/Dämonen und 7 Todsünden.

Der Beginn von "Sacra Terra" ist etwas "verstörend". Wie auch der Protagonist wähnt man sich kurz vor der Frage: Ist das hier ein Horrorfilm? Für Wimmelbild-Adventures, die eher auf "Mystery" / Märchen setzen, ist das Ambiente schon hier und da etwas "makaber". Trotzdem würde ich nicht so weit gehen um von "Grusel" oder "Horror" zu sprechen.

Relativ schnell ist man dann auch in seinem erwarteten und gewohnten Element: Gut oder weniger gut versteckte Objekte in Wimmelbildern finden oder (mehr oder weniger bekannte, meist faire, fast immer erklärte) Rätsel / Puzzle zu lösen und das Inventar mit losen Gegenständen vollzustopfen. Die Wimmelbilder sind ausnahmslos machbar, aber vereinzelt durchaus anstrengend. Überhaupt gilt: Je länger man das Spiel spielt, desto schwieriger dürfte die Konzentration sein. Einmal, bei einer dieser fiesen "Zahlen", wurden die Designer imo auch wirklich "unfair", so dass ich meinen ersten und einzigen "Tipp" nutzen musste, aber was solls. Es gibt sowieso kein Erfolgssystem.

Ein Tipp an alle: Macht nicht denselben Fehler wie ich! Das Spiel verfügt über eine Karte, auf der immer alle "aktiven Zonen" angezeigt werden. Nur dort gibt es was zu tun. Das hätte mir deutlich geholfen und das Spiel sicher noch mal 1 Stunde schneller gemacht. Leider scheint es keine Schnellreise zu geben (oder ich bin auch hier dumm...)
Ich habe das leider erst im Bonuskapitel herausgefunden, man kanns also auch so sehen: Auch ohne diesen starken Tipp war das Spiel ohne jede Lösungshilfe machbar (hat mich aber ein paar mal etliche Minuten rumlaufen lassen...)

Ansonsten gibts nicht viel zu sagen:
- Story ist "ok", die sind ja nie das Gelbe vom Ei. Zieht am Ende ganz schön an Geschwindigkeit an (da wollten sie wohl fertig werden... ;))
- Graphik ist schön.
- Es gibt in (fast) jeder Karte genau einen Bonusgegenstand. Das habe ich leider erst zu spät verstanden, ich dachte erst, die wären willkürlich. Wenn man wirklich Ausschau hält, sind sie leicht zu finden. Aber es gibt kaum nen Grund, warum man alle 42 finden sollte, zumindest habe ich keinen gefunden (wie gesagt, kein Erfolgssystem, weder Steam noch intern)

Fazit: Wer Wimmelbild-Spiele mag und mit etwas Horror/Blut kein Problem hat, findet hier ein grundsolides Spiel. Mit 2.99 € vor Rabatten auch nen echter Schnapp. Sicher keine Krone des Genres, aber das Spiel macht nichts falsch, also klare Empfehlung.

I'm speechless. Such a great hidden object game. Very good impression from the first seconds. And it's from 2011? - Unbelievable! It's ancient, but still so great. Visuals, animations, special effects, cutscenes are very good. Especially for HOGs.

Story is both thrilling and tragic. Music is exceptionally good and fits local grim atmosphere very well. And it captivates from the first chords.

There is some good variety of puzzles and min-games (some of them I see the first time) and a lot of HOG scenes. Really a lot. With lots of objects to find. And kinda tricky ones. Very often I was in a situation when I had to spend a good amount of time to find the last item from the list. There are also many hidden morphing collectibles to grab.

As to the cons - yeah, there are some. Absolutely not critical for me, but still. There is a good map, but that's just a map - you can't use if for fast travel. There is also no voice acting. At all. And no achievements. But it has trading cards. Overal - strongly recommend. I've already played few dozens of HOGs but this one still managed to impress me.
